arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: The government advocate stated that convicted sex offenders pose a serious threat to public safety.
The government advocate claimed Congress has authority to impose both criminal and civil sanctions for federal conduct.
The defendant advocate argued the government seeks to reach back after a federal sentence has expired.
The defendant advocate contended this brings a person back into federal control after returning to state authority.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The case tests the scope of federal power over individuals who have completed their federal sentences.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The Supreme Court heard oral argument in this case on April 17, 2013.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: The government wants the Court to uphold the registration mandate for this individual.
The defendant wants the Court to strike down the registration mandate for this individual.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The government argues Congress can impose civil sanctions to protect public safety after a federal conviction.
The defendant argues the government cannot reach back to control a person after their federal sentence expires.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Scalia asked if this power applies to all federal crimes, not just sex offenses.
Justice Sotomayor asked what limits exist on Congress imposing registration requirements for any federal conviction.
